clue.text: Looking at person going across cargo area

indicators.note: going across means the word for person spans the cargo area, which sits inside it

parts.note: a being is a person
the hold is where a ship or aircraft stows its cargo

explanation.surface: Someone watches a figure walk over a ship's loading bay.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to gaze upon or see something, in a slightly literary register, with the participle matching.

clue.text: Heart's tick — convulsive gasp coming up

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the joined pieces are read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: a tick is a moment in British informal speech, and a moment is shortened to mo
a sob is a convulsive catch of the breath

explanation.surface: A heartbeat is followed by a shuddering intake of breath rising in the chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns MO + SOB (MOSOB) upside down in this down entry. 'Tick' is British slang for a moment, as in 'half a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative synonym: the breast as the seat of feelings, as in a secret kept close to the chest.

clue.text: Severe law not yet ready — high standard set

parts.note: hard means severe, as in a hard winter
an Act of Parliament is a law
something still to come is promised 'to follow', like the details at the end of a news flash

explanation.surface: A strict statute is still being drafted, though the bar has been put high.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a performance so good that whoever comes next will struggle to match it.

clue.text: Vital period as corrupt file given to magazine

indicators.note: given to hands the rearranged word to the magazine, setting it in front of the title
corrupt data is scrambled, so the letters of the word that follows are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Time is the American weekly news magazine

explanation.surface: At a crucial moment a damaged computer document is handed to a periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrupt' rearranges FILE into LIFE, and 'given to' sets it beside the magazine. Vital here means 'of the living', not 'crucial'.
explanation.definitionFit: Witty paraphrase: vital means relating to being alive, so the span a person is alive is a vital stretch.

clue.text: Poor country loses a decent man

indicators.note: loses tells you the country's name gives up the letter named next

parts.note: India is a country
a gent is a gentleman, a man of decent behaviour

explanation.surface: An impoverished nation is deprived of a good fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both adjectives describe someone needy, lacking the means to live.

clue.text: Try a shirt: it hangs off you

parts.note: a go is a try, as in have a go
a tee is a T-shirt

explanation.surface: A shopper is told to put on a garment that turns out far too loose.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'it' the baggy shirt; the definition is really a small beard dangling from the chin.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: a small pointed beard that dangles from the wearer's chin.

clue.text: Expensive at either end with runs, loud shout to dispense with a slip

indicators.note: both ends of the word carry the same letter, and that single letter is taken

parts.note: R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: to dispense with something is to do without it, so the shout gives up the letter named next

parts.note: a roar is a loud shout

explanation.surface: A costly spell of cricket, full of scoring and yelling, where one close fielder could be spared.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests cricket, where a slip is a close fielder; here it is a mistake. 'at either end' takes the E that opens and closes 'Expensive'; 'to dispense with' drops A from ROAR, leaving ROR.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a small mistake, as in a careless lapse of the pen.

clue.text: Car's condition

definitions.meaning: the British name for a station wagon, a car with a long load space behind the seats
a person's state or standing in life, the older sense kept in marriage-service language

explanation.definitionFit: Both are dictionary senses: a long-bodied load-carrying car in Britain, and an old word for one's rank or standing.

clue.text: Evil dwarf we hear ruffles and starts to upset family

indicators.note: we hear tells you the word for ruffles is taken by its sound and spelt differently

parts.note: rumples means ruffles or creases
something that tilts is beginning to tip over
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: A wicked little man is reported to cause a stir and begin to distress relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' looks like a first-letters signal but is plain meaning: what starts to upset TILTS. 'we hear' respells RUMPLES as its sound-alike RUMPELS.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Grimm fairy-tale imp who spins straw into gold and demands the queen's child.

clue.text: Right to drink retsina, wrong to show self-control

indicators.note: to drink is to take in, so the abbreviation takes the rearranged word inside it

parts.note: RT is an abbreviation of right, as in Rt Hon

indicators.note: wrong says the letters of the word before it are out of order and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hedonist's motto: Greek wine is fine, moderation is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a drinker's motto, with 'Right' and 'wrong' as moral verdicts. Really 'wrong' jumbles the Greek pine-resin wine into ESTRAIN, and 'to drink' wraps an abbreviation round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: holding oneself back and keeping one's impulses in check.

clue.text: Given stalks to eat lost weight and shot up

indicators.note: lost says the abbreviation that follows goes missing from the phrase before it

parts.note: an animal given dried stalks to eat is straw-fed

explanation.surface: Someone put on a diet of stems slimmed down and then grew rapidly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot up' reads as grew quickly but means raked with gunfire. 'lost' removes W from STRAW-FED.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: attacked with gunfire from low-flying aircraft, which is to rake a place with bullets.

clue.text: Among non-science subjects, one the writer recalled is divinity

indicators.note: Among puts what follows the comma inside the subjects named first

parts.note: the arts are the non-science subjects at school or university

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the pair of pieces before it runs backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
the writer of the clue, speaking of themself, is me

explanation.surface: Of the humanities, the one the author remembers is theology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divinity' looks like the school subject, sitting neatly beside the humanities, but it means a goddess. 'recalled' gives EMI, which 'Among' tucks inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon is a deity.

clue.text: Tried to indicate average temperature

parts.note: the mean is the arithmetic average
T is the physics abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Someone attempted to point out the typical reading on a thermometer.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a speaker who intended a certain sense was attempting to convey it.

clue.text: Newcomer to pub said to have hazarded what a body was on

indicators.note: said tells you the two words that follow are spoken, then respelt as their sound-alikes

parts.words: hazarded what a body was on
parts.note: to hazard a guess is to venture one, so hazarded is guessed; a bier is the stand on which a corpse or coffin rests

explanation.surface: A stranger in the bar reportedly ventured an opinion about where a corpse had lain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newcomer to pub' suggests a person; it is a visiting ale, one from an outside brewery on sale for a short time. 'said' makes GUESSED BIER the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Witty description: an ale from an outside brewery sold temporarily in a British bar, so newly arrived on the counter.

clue.text: Element some miser hoarded

indicators.note: hoarded means stashed away, so the miser's name is stored inside the word for some

parts.note: any means some, as in 'have you any change?'
Timon of Athens, Shakespeare's embittered recluse who digs up a hoard of gold, is the setter's miser, though strictly a misanthrope

explanation.surface: A skinflint stashed away a quantity of some chemical substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' tempts you to look for a hidden word, but 'hoarded' is a container signal. Shakespeare's recluse is better known as a man-hater than a miser, though he does dig up gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the brittle silvery metalloid with symbol Sb is one of the chemical substances in the periodic table.

clue.text: Make fast all but the last hoist: I swear, making this

indicators.note: all but the last keeps every letter of the word for make fast except its final one

parts.note: to affix is to fasten or make fast
a davit is a small crane that hoists a ship's boats

explanation.surface: A sailor secures every sling except the final one and vows that he is doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all but the last' drops X from AFFIX. The definition is spoken by the person making the document: whoever produces one swears to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a written statement sworn on oath, so the person producing it is swearing.

clue.text: Like it to knock back?

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons

indicators.note: to knock back is to send backwards, so the two-letter word before it is turned round

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A host asks whether a guest fancies downing a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'to knock back' turns IT into TI, and also means to drink quickly, which suits a sparkling Italian wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusive description: an Italian sparkling white wine is something one might enjoy drinking down.

clue.text: To minimise danger, secure container for child?

definitions.meaning: to take no risks and choose the cautious course
a whimsical coinage on the model of playpen or playhouse: a strongbox meant for a child's games

explanation.surface: A parent reduces risk by putting a child in a sturdy enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: One is the idiom for avoiding risk; the other fancifully imagines a toy strongbox for a youngster.

clue.text: Newton's apple perhaps an unexpected bit of luck

definitions.meaning: fruit blown down from the tree, like the apple said to have dropped beside Newton
a sudden gain nobody was counting on, such as an inheritance

explanation.surface: The apple that inspired Newton may have been a stroke of good fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally fruit the breeze brings down, and figuratively any unlooked-for gain, a sense that grew from the literal one.

clue.text: Feature of arctic line held by enemy

indicators.note: held by says the abbreviation for line sits inside the word for enemy

parts.note: a foe is an enemy

explanation.surface: A polar boundary is occupied by hostile forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a sheet of floating sea ice is typical of polar waters.

clue.text: In a catalogue, stick climber

indicators.note: In places the word for stick inside the two-word phrase for a catalogue

parts.note: a list is a catalogue
to pin something is to stick or fasten it

explanation.surface: A gardener pastes a picture of a climbing plant into a brochure.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a mountaineer, originally one who scales peaks in the Alps.

clue.text: Heal, and marry again

definitions.meaning: to mend or make whole once more
whimsically, to couple up a second time, taking the word as a prefix for again plus a verb for joining two together

explanation.surface: A wish for someone to recover and then wed a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: One is the ordinary sense of mending; the other is a jokey reading as joining in a couple once more.

clue.text: Took to the door such a shotgun, being heartless

indicators.note: heartless means lacking a heart, so the word describing the shotgun gives up its middle letter

parts.note: a shotgun with its barrel cut short is described as sawn-off

explanation.surface: A callous householder answered a knock carrying a firearm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being heartless' removes the middle letter N from SAWN-OFF. The surface has someone carrying a gun to the door; really they escorted a guest out.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to see a departing visitor on their way is to accompany them out, here in the past tense.

clue.text: What's roamed around in desert?

indicators.note: in puts the rearranged letters inside the word for desert

parts.note: desert as an adjective means arid, that is dry

indicators.note: around says the letters of the word before it move about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A riddle asking which creature has wandered the sandy wastes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole question is both definition and wordplay: 'around' gives ROMEDA and 'in' places it, while the sentence as a whole describes a camel's life.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the one-humped Arabian camel is an animal that wanders arid sandy regions.

clue.text: Day-long channel

parts.note: to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: A television station that broadcasts from morning to night.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen hides the join: 'Day' and 'long' work separately, and 'long' is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a trench dug to carry water away is a drainage course.

clue.text: Feeling hot meal needs no starter

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

indicators.note: a starter opens a meal, so the meal's name goes without its opening letter

parts.note: lunch is the midday meal

explanation.surface: Someone senses that a warm dinner can do without a first course.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an intuitive sense about something, a suspicion held without proof.

clue.text: One potentially explosive book half concealed by accountant, isn't it?

indicators.note: with half of it concealed, only the front half of the word for book stays in view

parts.note: a volume is a book
CA is a chartered accountant, the Scottish professional title
the tag question 'isn't it?' can be swapped for 'no?' at the close of a sentence

explanation.surface: A bookkeeper has partly hidden a ledger that could blow up in someone's face, surely?
explanation.walkthrough: 'half concealed' hides UME, the back half of VOLUME; 'by' sets what is left beside CA. 'isn't it?' is the tag question, which can also be said 'no?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a mountain that may erupt violently is a thing liable to blow up.

clue.text: What's in Montreal? Ask any American

indicators.note: What's in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what a Canadian city contains and is told any US citizen would know.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a resident of the forty-ninth US state is one kind of United States citizen.

clue.text: Defensive structure our side built into hill

indicators.note: built into says the word for our side is set inside the word for hill

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor in south-west England
our side, spoken of by its own members, is we

explanation.surface: Our troops raised a fortification on the slope.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a tall fortified building such as a keep is put up to resist attack.

clue.text: Broadcast cheerful news upfront? There's no such thing!

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it, so the letters that follow are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: upfront points to the letter at the front of the word news

explanation.surface: A radio station leads with good tidings, then insists such things don't exist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' rearranges CHEERFUL plus N, the letter 'upfront' takes from 'news'. The definition quotes the proverb that nothing is ever really given away.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: the proverb says a midday meal at no cost does not exist, since somebody always pays.
